problem: Prior social robot navigation methods are emotionally reactive (using only past gaits), ignore the robot's effect on pedestrian emotion, and use heuristic, fixed proxemic constraints that miss individual comfort space.
motivation: Robots in crowds must anticipate where pedestrians will go and how they feel, so they can keep socially acceptable distances. Predicting future gaits conditioned on perceived emotion, and adapting personal-space profiles per pedestrian, should give more comfortable navigation.
key_idea: Predict emotion-conditioned full-body pedestrian gait trajectories with a transformer, and feed them into an RL navigation policy with an adaptive Gaussian personal-space profile and an emotion-change penalty.
insight: Conditioning trajectory prediction on perceived emotion and using per-pedestrian emotion/orientation-scaled comfort space reduces personal space deviation versus baselines (10.2 vs 25.3 m in scenario 5). The gain costs some extra distance and time versus Crowdmove, which is a trade-off for social compliance. No ablation isolates the emotion context or the reward term, so the causal attribution is not tested.
method: Pose extraction: SAP-Net + TP-Net (Dabral et al.) extract 16-joint 3D gaits from RGB-D video.
Emotion Context Network: grouped-convolution multi-view classifier (from ProxEmo) on gait image embeddings, giving probabilities over happy/sad/angry/neutral.

Transformer trajectory forecaster: 6-layer encoder-decoder over linearly embedded gaits; emotion probabilities are multiplied element-wise with the encoder output before decoder cross-attention, assuming constant emotion over the horizon.
Adaptive proxemic Gaussian: an oriented Gaussian per pedestrian, scaled by comfort multiplier C_i (emotion-weighted radii from psychology times a view-group constant).
RL policy: encodes 3 LiDAR scans (512 each), 18 historical+predicted skeleton poses (as images), previous velocity and goal, and outputs continuous v in [0,1] and w in [-1,1].
Reward: goal progress/arrival + collision penalty + rotation smoothness penalty + penalty when pedestrian emotion turns negative (angry/sad).
Training: multi-stage in the Stage simulator, first without obstacles and then with obstacles and 5-50 pedestrians with emotions and gaits from gait datasets.

setting.backbone: Transformer encoder-decoder (trajectory forecaster) + grouped-CNN emotion classifier + CNN/MLP RL policy (all trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Emotion-labelled gait datasets (Randhavane 342 + Bhattacharya 1835 = 2177 samples); walking/running samples from NTU RGB+D 60 and PoseTrack for the forecaster; Stage simulator scenarios for RL
setting.observation: RGB-D camera (3D skeletal poses) + 2D LiDAR scans (3 frames) + relative goal and velocity
setting.action_space: continuous translational (0-1) and rotational (-1 to 1) velocity

numbers_note: Not a standard embodied-navigation benchmark; results are on custom Stage scenarios 5 and 6 (distance, time, personal space deviation). The claimed intent-prediction MSE superiority over baselines is not tabulated in the text.
results: On custom Stage scenarios, the method has the lowest average personal space deviation: 10.2 vs 25.3 (Crowdmove) in scenario 5 and 32.8 vs 57.8 in scenario 6. Distance and time are slightly worse than Crowdmove (172.3 m vs 152.5 m in scenario 5) but better than RRT/PRM.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation on custom scenarios with 20 runs each; no real-robot experiments and no intent-prediction table or ablations
Emotion is assumed constant over the prediction horizon and only walking emotion is perceived; static pedestrians are not handled
Some baselines are mismatched (RRT/PRM planners) and the metric units for personal space deviation are unclear
builds_on: Giuliari et al. transformer trajectory prediction
Vega et al. adaptive spatial density
